html:
The Licinio-Sextian laws were a group of Roman laws passed around 367 BCE. They were proposed by two tribunes of the plebs, Gaius Licinius Stolo and Lucius Sextius Lateranus, after years of struggle, and they were a turning point in the Conflict of the Orders between patricians and plebeians.

According to Livy, the laws did three things:

  • Interest already paid on debts was taken off the amount still owed.
  • No one could hold more than a fixed amount, 500 iugera, of public land.
  • One of the two consuls, the chief magistrates, could be a plebeian.

In 366 BCE Sextius became the first plebeian consul. The patricians made up for it by creating new offices that at first only they could hold. Over the next decades plebeians opened up every office, ending with the Lex Hortensia in 287 BCE. Tradition links the old general Camillus with the settlement. The land limit was widely ignored, and two centuries later Tiberius Gracchus tried to enforce it again in his land law.
